extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters and art students (artists seeking guidance on depicting mountains and snow)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance for representing mountains (especially distant ranges, inferior/bedded hills, and snow on Alps) in landscape painting, covering form, structure, aerial effects, and brush/execution techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme-distance characteristics: sharp outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme distance of large objects always characterized by very sharp outline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a large object is at extreme distance its mass appears filmy or transparent but its edge becomes excessively keen—often 'as sharp as a knife' even when the interior detail is lost. Do not confuse softened or melting outlines (which indicate mist or improper focus) with the true effect of great distance. Examples: trees miles off become indistinguishable from rocks by their sharp silhouette; Turner consistently uses excessively sharp edges for very distant mountains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency/filminess combined with keen edges for distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distant masses should show transparency or filminess of mass together with excessive sharpness of edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both facts are 'invariably given' in effective distant passages. If you render a distant mass as opaque or with a blunt edge you create impossibilities (either the color is wrong for a near object, or the blunted edge is impossible for an extreme distance). Compare Claude (opacity and soft edges are wrong) with Turner (moist pale washes leaving a firm edge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaking slurred lines for distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Slurred or melting lines are not the characteristic of distant large objects unless there is mist/vapor or the eye's focus is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you soften an outline you must represent intervening mist or else bring the object closer and change aerial colors accordingly. Otherwise you depict an impossibility. (If you soften without mist you contradict the clear-air distant effect.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Turner's execution technique for extreme distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a very moist pale dash of color leaving a firm edge to render extreme distances; sometimes represented by actual outline only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner often applied moist pale washes (possibly working paper upside down) so the top edge dried as a very firm, almost linear edge. In some works (e.g., Battle of Marengo) he uses nothing more than an outline for extreme distance. This technique produces filminess of mass and a decisive, razor-like edge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and render the true character of snow
rubrics_metrics.description: Snow's forms, surface, transparency, and light-and-shade qualities must be studied rather than stylized as simple white rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fresh deep snow has exquisite curves, changeful surfaces, delicate transparency, sharp pale shadows of 'heavenly color', intense reflected lights, and occurrences of transmitted light. Represent snow wreaths, cornices, blue irregular cliffs, and the transitions to ice where appropriate. Avoid treating snow as mere white rock or powdering; avoid guessing from cloud shapes or exaggerating into impossible heights and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceive the underlying mountain anatomy before laying on snow
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists should first 'conceive the body beneath' and then lay the snow on it; an Alp is not merely a white mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snow is 'loaded on until the rocks can hold no more' and hangs in festoons and domes governed by the rock beneath and prevailing winds. Represent different snow conditions (coating, shallow incrustation, deep constrained snow, hanging festoons/cornices, overwhelming accumulation) and how they modify the underlying forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent types of snow accumulation and their curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Different snow-conditions (mere coating, shallow glaze, deep cramped snow, fractured festoons, pure sweeping accumulation) produce distinctive shapes and lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the snow's sweeping festoons, domes, and lines of drifting to emphasize curvature and to 'unite and oppose' the rock's broken lines. Convey wind direction effects and the way surplus snow forms avalanches and cornices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pictorial clichés and trivial local details
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not fill Alpine paintings with national or domestic clichés (chalets, cow-bells, buttermilk) or rely on superficial local color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the Alpine 'ideal' or 'spirit'—the pure and holy hills as a link between heaven and earth—rather than anecdotal or decorative motifs. Such trivial details weaken the grandeur and are bad practice unless serving a deliberate purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict stratification: two principal sets of lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferior (bedded) mountains are composed of layers; their contours commonly show two great sets of lines—surfaces of the beds and edges/terminations—often at right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the planes where beds emerge and the escarpments where their continuity is interrupted. These two systems of lines produce much of a mountain's character; indicate them clearly in the mass and in the patterning of light and shadow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show joints and block-like structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Most rocks are further divided by joints which throw the bed into blocks (often rhomboidal), producing even faces and clear angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent blocky, masonry-like faces and planar terminations of beds—avoid torn, ragged edges where joints should give even facets. Use these block divisions to organize the rock into believable, solid masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render lines of lamination in nearer views
rubrics_metrics.description: Laminar lines divide rock into delicate plates or layers; they often cross strata and are conspicuous in near views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include fine lamination lines on faces and fragments (e.g., roofing slate behavior) because they affect breakage, edge character, and near detail. These lines give texture and should vary in direction and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor natural tendencies but allow variety (laws are tendencies not absolutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of mountain form are universal tendencies evidenced by many instances, not rigid rules applicable without exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While composing, aim to show the aggregate tendencies (e.g., boughs droop lower as they are lower on the trunk; lines of stratification predominate), but introduce variety and exceptions so the scene feels natural. Do not enforce a monotonous, mechanical regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest parallelism without mechanical repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the parallelism of beds and recurring structural lines, but avoid repeating identical marks or lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's Loch Coriskin demonstrates how a multitude of varied lines can still express rigid parallelism. Achieve the sense of repetition and unity through varied repetition—never by cloning the same stroke—so the eye perceives order without monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brushwork must imply form, substance, and light—not meaningless pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Brush marks should represent rock forms, shadows, and reflected light; they should not be ornamental 'touches' without meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comma-shaped or square daubs that merely pattern the surface. Dark sides must cast shadows, show reflected light, fissures and substance. If brushwork breaks the light, it must return information about form; otherwise it becomes 'pure, staring paint' and undermines fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicularity increases toward summits; skeleton tends to concave curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines by which rocks are terminated become steeper (more vertical) as we approach the summit; distant ranges tend to series of concave curves meeting in peaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose distant ranges as sweeping, concave valleys with angular peaks rather than rounded convex summits. Represent greater perpendicularity at higher elevations, except where specific geology or erosion suggests otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aqueous erosion produces gentle convex domes and uniform slopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Aqueous action tends to make large elevated surfaces symmetrically convex and dome-like, descending to an average slope (~40 degrees) and then a uniform straight descent to the valley.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In lower mountain parts, indicate broad, symmetrical convex curves and consistent slopes shaped by soil wash. Interrupt these forms with cliffs and projecting masses that reveal internal stratification, but keep the overall convex simplicity where water action dominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torrent erosion: furrows, ravines and hierarchical ridges
rubrics_metrics.description: Streams delicately furrow mountains from summits into multitudinous threads that unite into ravines; where rock is soft this process subdivides masses into buttresses and successively finer ridges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict the fine uppermost stream threads and their aggregation into larger ravines; show how ridges become steeper and narrower upward and are themselves subdivided. Use these patterns to imply erosion history and material softness/hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance broad unity of mass with multiplicity of detail and hierarchical grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains should present a 'broad and bold simplicity of mass' while also containing 'excessive complication of details' grouped into subordinate divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose large unifying forms that carry the scene's energy, and populate them with countless individual touches that suggest smaller hills, crags and distances—each touch should feel momentary and then melt into the common line. Organize details into progressively larger groupings (minor features → groups → vast dynasties) to produce convincing scale and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid isolated, unconnected heap-like hills (show association and connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw hills as separate, conflicting, shapeless heaps with no marking of distances or divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the association, connection and divisions in a mountain mass so that valleys, distances, and hierarchy of parts are apparent. Ancient art's failure is cited as an anti-pattern: disconnected petty heaps produce smallness and contemptible appearance.
